newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-MIM shakeup seen sending mixed signals.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-MIM shakeup seen sending mixed signals.

text.p: Recent top-level management upheavals at MIM Holdings Ltd including the departure on Tuesday of Mt Isa operations chief Phil Wright has spooked investors with memories of former executive blood-letting at the base metals giant.

Wright's resignation, which followed hard on the heels of two other top executives' dismissals, echoed events of 1995 which saw the departure of chief executive Norm Fussell and the arrival of former Comalco Ltd executive Nick Stump, share analysts told Reuters.
"Stump is now firmly in control. Wright's resignation was seen by the market as a dismissal. That's why the share price went down," a Sydney-based analyst said.

MIM shares have dropped from A$1.77 on Monday, the day before Wright's departure was announced, to A$1.69 at 0145 GMT (12.45 p.m.) on Thursday, exactly mid-way between its 12-month high of A$1.98 and its low of A$1.40.
But other analysts saw Wright's resignation in another light.
"Part of his (Stump's) philosophy is to restructure management to become more proactive and responsive," John Webby, senior resources analyst at broker Wilson HTM Ltd, said.
"Stump wants to change the management culture and get MIM on a cost-competitive basis in a world environment," he said.

This philosophy brought about the departure of Wright, responsible for the revival of fortunes at MIM's Mt Isa operations, as well as the departures of Geoff Billard as head of the metals division and Ross Fardon as exploration manager, Webby said.
Stump has spent the last two days, allaying market fears that more executive blood was to be spilt as part of MIM's major restructuring programme.
"I expect no more management changes," Stump told Reuters on Wednesday.
Wright's resignation was a "confluence of events" with the role of Mt Isa manager no longer for "a reformer but an operator-builder," Stump said.
He dismissed analysts' views that Wright's departure was the latest in a series of executive sackings aimed at stamping the chief executive's position of authority.
"I wanted a commitment for two to three years. I knew Phil was not going to stay another two to three years," Stump said.

Another Sydney-based analyst, who declined to be named, said the market would absorb MIM's management shake-up, as long as the Mt Isa management team remain focused on Wright's already firm direction.
MIM was spending A$500 million developing the new Enterprise copper mine as well as the Ernest Henry copper-gold mine and was well advanced at the massive Alumbrera copper mine in Argentina.
"A lot of this, including Alumbrera, was the result of Phil Wright's groundwork," the analyst said.
"The new man a Mt Isa, Stephen O'Donnell, has a very good team already in place," he said.
